newsitem.title: USA: Clinton-Yeltsin meeting highlights summit opening.
newsitem.headline: Clinton-Yeltsin meeting highlights summit opening.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin meet on the sidelines of the summit of leading industrial nations on Friday to discuss European security issues, arms control and Russia's integration into the global economy.
The meeting, several hours before the Group of Seven summit opens, will be the third between Clinton and Yeltsin this year.
Clinton will also hold separate talks with French President Jacques Chirac and Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi during the day.

U.S. officials said Clinton and Yeltsin would continue a dialogue on NATO's planned expansion and its new friendly relationship with Moscow. On arms control and economic integration, the other main items on their agenda, the U.S. and Russian leaders appeared to have little progress to celebrate.

The Russian parliament shows no signs of ratifying the 1990 START 2 nuclear reduction agreement. While Clinton remains committed to supporting Russian membership in international institutions like the World Trade Organisation (WTO), there is little movement on that front either.

"We're making progress with Russia, but it has not yet formulated its market access offers," U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky told reporters. "Ideally, we would like Russia to be able to move quickly, but the substance is not there yet."

In a gesture meant to underline Yeltsin's enhanced role at the Denver summit, U.S. officials said Clinton had arranged for the Russian president to lead off the discussion at the first event of the three-day gathering, a working dinner on Friday evening.

The dinner will take place at the Phipps Conference Centre, a Georgian mansion set on a 5-1/2 acre (2.2 hectare) estate that once belonged to Colorado philanthropist and onetime senator Lawrence Phipps.

Much of the dinner discussion was expected to focus on Bosnia. Yeltsin and leaders of the G7 -- the United States, Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan -- were expected to focus on what they can do "to advance the non- military parts of the peace process" in the former Yugoslav region, White House official Dan Tarullo said.

The United States is pressing its partners in Bosnia to place greater emphasis on rebuilding democratic institutions in the war-ravaged country in order to pave the way for the scheduled withdrawal of an international peace-keeping force by the middle of next year.
